newsitem.title: UK: Strong sales improve odds of August UK rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Strong sales improve odds of August UK rate rise.

text.p: An unexpected surge in annual retail sales growth in June has increased the chances of a 25-basis-point increase in Britain's 6.75 percent official interest rate next month, the fourth such rise in as many months, analysts say.

"It will put yet more pressure on the Bank of England to tighten again in August," said CIBC chief economist David Coleman. "They should really have done 50 basis points last time, but since they didn't we'll get 25 again next month."
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee is due to meet on August 6 and 7.

UK June retail sales grew by 0.6 percent compared with the previous month and expectations of an increase of 0.4 percent. But the real shock was the rise in the annual rate to 5.4 percent after predictions of a slowdown to 4.5 percent.
Analysts said that revisions to back data explained the size of the gap between forecasts and the actual outcome.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) revised the index for retail sales for June 1996, down to 110.6 from 111.2.

"The sales figures are clear signs of how strong consumer demand is at the moment and coming in a month where the consumer confidence indicators are also strong, the odds are we will see a rate rise at the next meeting," said HSBC economist Dharshini David.

British consumers have seen a surge in their spending power following windfall payments totalling 30 billion stg from building society mergers and flotations and analysts say the sales data show they are prepared to spend it.

The ONS said there was little detailed evidence on spending of windfall payments but said windfall cash would be expected to be used largely for purchases of household goods, where sales rose dramatically in June.
Household goods spending leapt by 21 percent year on year in June, whilst spending on clothing and footwear -- another barometer of the strength of consumer demand -- gained 4.4 percent.
The annual rise in household spending was last higher in January 1988, when it was 22.1 percent, the ONS said.

The retail sales numbers have intensified the policy dilemma between the domestic demand led consumer and service sector and the tradable goods sector clobbered by the strength of sterling, which stormed to eight-year heights against the deutschemark after today's data release.

The pound soared to 3.08 marks, its strongest level since September 1989, and analysts say that if anything persuades the Bank of England to hold off from raising rates next month it will be fear that this will gives the pound even more support.
"We've already seen the manufacturing sector is coming under enormous pressure from the pound that has strengthened even more since the committee last met," IBJ chief economist Stephen Hannah said.

"I think it is a pretty close call as to whether they raise rates and intensify this dilemma on the foreign exchanges in August. I think they will have to raise rates again before the end of the year but whether they do so in August is a bit of a moot point," he said.

The Bank of England MPC said in the minutes of the June meeting, at which it raised interest rates by 25 basis points, that delaying a rate rise would make little difference to sterling and that uncertainties about the outcome of EMU were actually fuelling the currency's gains.
But the pound's recent performance could persuade them to take more account of the currency, Credit Lyonnais economist Glenn Davies said.

"My view is that they are not going to move in August I think that the strength of the pound has to now start to feature in the monetary policy decision I think as we move through this month and on into August we may see the pound trade back down a little," he said.
"But on three to six month view it looks to me as if the pound's going to stay very strong."

CIBC's Coleman is moving his year end forecast for base rates up to 7.5 percent from 7.25 percent but HSBC'S David is sticking with 7.0 percent, arguing that the inflation risks from high spending are being partially offset by consumers' continued reluctance to stomach higher prices.

Retail sales volumes in the second quarter, up 5.3 percent on an annual basis, are growing at their fastest rate since December 1988, the height of the consumer boom but the comparisons break down on the inflation front, according to NatWest Markets UK economist John O'Sullivan.
"The small gap between retail sales values(at 6.2 percent year on year) and volumes (at 5.4 percent) testifies to the near absence of price pressures on the high street," he said.
"At the moment, the sharp pick-up in demand is being easily absorbed at the retails stage, without driving up prices," he said.
--Cheryl Juckes, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5109
